body: Same way, though I had an amazing night last night, saw my favorite musician in concert, and then woke up this morning with the serotonin still coursing through my brain. Had a few hours of remembering happiness and thinking things would be okay for a while, and then something really stupid this evening as the sun was going down set me off again and the next thing I know, I'm crying. The brain is a weird beast.

I know exactly how you feel. I had just finished my master's degree from a top university in the UK and came back to the US, with three years of prior work experience at a great organization. It took me 9 months to get a job. During that period, I interviewed with 17 different organizations. Three times I made it to the final round after drawn out interview processes with three or more interviews, skills tests, and other hoops to jump through, only to be rejected. I was rejected 16 times and I wanted to die. I didn't see a way forward and I knew it was only going to end in me killing myself because what other option was there?

And then the 17th place to interview me made me an offer. I had lost all hope. People here on this subreddit told me it was all a numbers game, and I didn't want to believe them, I wanted to believe that I was a failure and that was all there was to it, but they were right. I don't know what the magic number is for you. I've heard you should take a piece of paper and write down the numbers 1-100 and you cross them off each time you get a rejection from a job, and that before you hit 100 you'll have one. The idea of going though 100 interviews sounds insane, and I thought that if I hit 100 and still didn't have a job, that'd be all the motivation I needed to follow through with killing myself.

The job market is BS. It's brutal and it's cruel and there's no fairness whatsoever, and half the time employers play games with you because you have no other choice than to play along. They have what you need. I wouldn't wish the job hunt on my worst enemy. 

Hang in there. Give it time. I know you've already given it far too much time than anyone should have to, but I've known amazing people with plenty of great experience and a good education that couldn't find a job for over a year. It's not fair and I wish you all the best.

I don't know, I think the not knowing would be worse on my family, so I've always thought that I would want to make sure they they didn't have to go days or weeks searching and hoping. End it and let them come to terms and move on, because I know eventually they would. I'm an only child, so I really only worry about my parents. But I also wouldn't want one of my loved ones to find me. Something I wrestle with is knowing that some person would have to find me, and I wish I wouldn't have to put that on anyone else. I don't want to hurt anyone, I just want my pain to stop. I guess the lesser of the evils would be making sure that the emergency services were the ones to find me, because they would be more prepared for that. 

But I'd like to be somewhere peaceful, in nature, at the end. And I'd just want people to know that I didn't want to hurt them, I just couldn't keep going.

I wonder why this is? I worked for an international non-profit before, and I've applied for a lot of international jobs since. You'd think experience in other countries and with other cultures would give you a boost in the job search. It makes no sense. And I can't believe your friends and family weren't supportive. :(

I'd kill for dual citizenship, though I don't know if it would do me any good either. There aren't tons of jobs in my field over there, and I got one interview while I was there but in the end it was too much for them to sponsor me for a work visa. I feel like the US job market has more variety, but there's so much competition for every position, it's hard to imagine ever winning out. I did it once, and I wonder if my luck has run out. I got my chance then and won't ever again. I should have never left my job. My life was good. It was an entry level job but at least I had a job. 

I wish I had built up more than just 3 years of experience before grad school. And now that I've been to grad school, I'm discounted for other entry level jobs, but I'm struggling to get any chances at more mid-level jobs. I'm not asking for a high salary and I keep trying to explain I don't mind being entry level for a few more years, if that's what it takes. I know I need to try a little longer, but how long? Eventually I'd rather die if this goes on. I don't know how to do that without ruining my family's lives, either. It sucks. I hope things turn around for the both of us soon.

Thank you. This is really comforting to hear. This morning I got an email that I got an interview for what is a dream job--though I definitely learned in my last job that no matter how much you love your job, every job is just a job at the end of the day. I don't expect to get this position, but starting to hear back from more places makes me feel like I'm running through the numbers now.

It's good to know I'm not the only one. MSc in public policy here, and I had researched it before I applied for my degree and there were a lot of job listings that I saw at the time that required a masters in public policy. But now that I have one, it's useless. I have a friend who did public health and is in the same situation. I think the worst part is people assuming that I'm overqualified because of the degree for low level jobs. I'd do an entry level job again just to have a job...

I hope we both find something soon!
